newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US retail sales seen up 0.6 pct in Feb.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US retail sales seen up 0.6 pct in Feb.

text.p: U.S. retail sales were seen rising by 0.6 percent in February, perhaps boosted somewhat by faster processing of income tax returns, economists said.

Analysts polled by Reuters expected, on average, that February retail sales would rise 0.6 percent, and by 0.7 percent excluding automobiles. The Commerce Department will release the data Thursday at 830 EST/1330 GMT.

"Car unit sales were off a little from the high level in January so we're guessing autos didn't boost the number. But retailers had a pretty good month," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Glassman said income tax refunds ran about $3.0 billion stronger in than normal in January, a factor that could lead to a stronger number than fundamentals would indicate.

"That's not the dominant factor. Job growth and income growth are stronger so spending is up," Glassman said. At February's expected pace, retail sales would rise by about 4.0 percent on an annualized basis.

If the data comes in as strong as forecast, Glassman said, it could make Federal Reserve policy-makers anxious because an annual retail sales growth rate of 4.0 percent would exceed their target. However, without obvious indicators of growing inflation, it would make it harder for the Fed to justify a tightening of monetary policy.
"It may be further evidence of the wealth effect playing itself out," Glassman said as many individuals may begin to spend some of the gains they have reaped in the stock market's recent runup.

"There's plenty of reason for the Fed to want to take out some insurance (in the form of a tightening of monetary policy), but their dilemma is rapid growth that still isn't straining inflation," Glassman said.
Ken Goldstein, economist with the Conference Board, said consumers currently have money to spend with more individuals working for higher wages.

"The work week is going up, wages are getting higher and consumers more confident. There was terrific housing growth in 1996 and consumers have not finished putting furnishings into those houses," Goldstein said.
Goldstein said Wall Street economists attributed too much of the 500,000 jobs created in January and February to the weather.

"Job growth in factories picked up and that's not weather related. Wall Street keeps scratching its head, but if ever you needed a textbook example in 1987 when the stock market fell 500 points you never saw a dribble in the trend rate of consumer spending," Goldstein said.
Wage and non-labor costs both are rising, Goldstein noted. As productivity gains tail off profit margins will have to shrink or prices will have to rise, he said.
While the inevitable pickup in inflation wasn't likely to be seen in the next batch of consumer and producer price indices, it will surface soon, he said.
He saw yields on the 30-year bond rising to 7.1 to 7.2 percent, providing the trigger for the Fed to tighten rates.

Unlike most economists, however, he said the Fed would "jump in with both feet" and tighten by 50 to 100 basis points, most likely 75 basis points. Most analysts expect the Fed to tighten by only 25 basis points, either at the policy-making FOMC's March 25 or May 20 meeting.
